4.5. Metrics for a Key Performance Indicator (KPI)

You should agree metrics with the successful supplier to hold them accountable for delivering their social value commitments. You should use the standard reporting metrics if they are provided for the sub-criteria you have selected. If they are not provided, you should adapt the standard reporting metrics or agree new reporting metrics with the supplier. You should adapt or agree new metrics if reporting against them would be discriminatory when applied to a treaty-state supplier.

You should ensure any KPI or performance indicator is a combination of a deliverable target and a reported numeric value which you will use to measure the delivery of the target. The standard reporting metrics have been designed in this way. You should also ensure that your awarded contract has the provisions needed to ensure you can collect the data required, and seek the supplier’s permission to publish this data if you need this.

You should incorporate the Social Value Model commitments set out in the winning supplier’s bid into your contract. For contracts valued at £5 million or more[footnote 12], set at least one Social Value Model KPI. You should set and publish this KPI on the Central Digital Platform in addition to the three KPIs that may be required by the Procurement Act[footnote 13]. If you cannot publish using the Central Digital Platform, you should make arrangements to publish the Social Value Model KPI elsewhere. You are also encouraged to set a Social Value Model KPI in contracts with a value below £5m to monitor social value delivery if appropriate.

You should develop suitable reporting thresholds and a methodology to determine performance, for example:

Good: The supplier is meeting or exceeding the social value KPI targets and/or deliverables to agreed milestones

Approaching target: The supplier is close to meeting the social value KPI targets to agreed milestones

Requires improvement: The supplier’s performance is below the social value KPI targets or behind schedule

Inadequate: The supplier’s performance is significantly below the social value KPI targets or behind schedule

Other: Performance cannot be described as good, approaching target, requires improvement or inadequate (further information here[footnote 14])

These ratings should be appropriate to the contract and Social Value Model outcome. You can adjust the ratings before or during the contract lifecycle to reflect wider circumstances or to challenge the supplier to achieve better outcomes, become more efficient, or innovative over time.

You should ensure that the monitoring and reporting of social value outcomes is appropriate and feasible, and whether it provides a suitable incentive for the supplier without being overly burdensome. Use the information you gained during the ‘Define’ stage to assess the capability of the supplier to deliver, monitor, and report KPIs. If performance cannot be assessed using a KPI appropriately, you should consider setting performance indicator targets or other contractual terms which bind the supplier to delivering social value outcomes.

You should ensure the details of any social value KPIs are included in your contract details notice when this is published.

5. Manage

The ‘Manage’ stage of the commercial lifecycle is where you monitor performance of the contract, build beneficial relationships with your suppliers, and ensure that contractual obligations are being met, resolving any issues or disputes if needed.

5.1. Manage deliverables

You should engage regularly with your suppliers to ensure they are meeting contractual requirements and monitor their performance against the social value KPIs or performance indicators. If a supplier struggles to meet expectations, you should investigate how it will resolve issues. You should agree changes to KPIs or performance indicators if needed to ensure they remain an appropriate measure of the supplier’s performance.

In exceptional circumstances, you should remind suppliers that evidence of poor performance against the social value KPIs can be used to exclude them from bidding on future contracts.

5.2. Publish a contract performance notice

You should publish a contract performance notice on the Central Digital Platform at least every 12 months for contracts worth £5m or more. This should include the supplier’s performance against the social value KPIs, in addition to any other KPIs set for the contract. You can use the publication of the contract performance notice as an opportunity to engage with the supplier and ensure they continue to meet expectations.

In the event that a contracting authority considers that a supplier is not performing a public contract to its satisfaction (and the supplier has been given a proper opportunity to improve performance but failed to do so), they should publish information containing the details of the failure to perform.[footnote 15] The supplier can then, at contracting authorities’ discretion and if the circumstances giving rise to the poor performance are continuing or likely to occur again, be excluded from future procurements.[footnote 16]

5.3. Quarterly social value reporting

If the Social Value Model’s standard reporting metrics have been used, central government departments should report the numerical and social value KPI attainment data to the Cabinet Office each financial quarter. This data is used to assess how frequently each Social Value Model outcome, criteria, and sub-criteria is applied in procurements and how successfully suppliers deliver against their commitments.

Public sector staff can access training at the Government Commercial College and attend Cabinet Office Community of Practice webinars. The cross-government Social Value Network shares knowledge and best practice across central government departments. Departments should nominate a lead representative to share this knowledge across their organisation, executive agencies, and non-departmental public bodies. To join the network, please contact info@gca.gov.uk.

2.2. Procurement pipeline plan

You should speak to procurement, commercial, and finance teams to identify procurements in your pipeline that:

have a total contract value of £1m or more [footnote 3]

will have a tender notice published on or after 1 January 2027

will be awarded under the Procurement Act 2023

Identifying future procurement activity helps you to identify key markets you buy from regularly and conduct better preliminary market engagement with suppliers and other stakeholders. Engaging with the market early gives bidders the best chance to understand what will be expected of them, so they can submit a high quality tender.

For procurements with a tender notice published before 1 January 2027, you are encouraged to apply PPN 026. However, you can use an earlier Social Value Model from before this date if applying PPN 026 would invalidate previous market engagement activities.

PPN 026 does not apply to utilities contracts awarded by private utilities[footnote 4] or to contracts where the primary purpose is overseas delivery (for example, overseas embassies). However, private utilities are encouraged to apply this PPN to help achieve jobs and skills objectives through their procurements.

3. Define

In the ‘Define’ stage you will identify appropriate Social Value Model outcomes, criteria, sub-criteria, and metrics to include in your procurement documents. You should engage with all stakeholders to understand their expectations and capability for delivering social value outcomes.

3.1. Assess the market

You should determine the market maturity for delivering successful Social Value Model outcomes in the markets you buy from. Many suppliers and industry groups actively promote their social value activities which can help you understand market capability. You should also consider the market’s cost structure, particularly its labour and bought-in costs, because this may impact the Social Value Model outcome most appropriate for your contract.

Trade unions are important stakeholders that contracting authorities can engage to support the selection of outcomes and sub-criteria where relevant to the procurement. Where an independent trade union or independent unions are recognised by companies operating in a relevant sector , you should consider engaging these unions. Where no union is recognised, you may search for relevant independent unions, for example by using the TUC’s Union Finder tool.

You should determine the likelihood of international suppliers bidding on the contract. You should be aware of how your procurement may impact the UK’s international obligations, including the prohibition on conditions or undertakings which encourage local development. You have a legal duty to ensure that the Social Value Model commitments within your contract comply with these obligations, including by not discriminating against or deterring treaty state suppliers from bidding on your contract. Discrimination arises where a treaty state supplier is treated less favourably than a UK supplier. In the social value context, discrimination is likely to arise where a treaty state supplier cannot bid on your contract or is deterred from doing so by, for example, higher costs or practical obstacles. You must not apply PPN 026 to your procurement if it would breach your duty to treaty-state suppliers.

You may find it helpful to keep records of previous market assessments, pre-market engagement, and attainment against social value metrics. This will help you determine what works well and where you can improve the delivery of Social Value Model outcomes.

If the contract will be delivered in a specific location, you may find it helpful to understand the needs of the local community. This includes identifying the target cohorts who would most benefit from good jobs and skills relevant to the contract, or who face barriers to entering the contract workforce. You can find information to support this in Annex E.

Where possible, and consistent with the UK’s international obligations, you should consider how the Social Value Model can be used to support the delivery of jobs, skills and opportunities for the target cohorts in contracts that are not location specific.

Health can be a key factor in whether people can enter, remain in, and progress in work. Worsening physical or mental health can lead to weaker economic growth and reduced labour supply. When applying the Social Value Model, you should consider whether proposed activities are likely to benefit target cohorts and communities experiencing poorer health outcomes, long-term health conditions, disabilities or health-related barriers to employment.

Evaluating if suppliers have policies that encourage employees to stay, such as embedded training and development programmes or routes for progression, can support job retention.

The government wants to create new jobs and skills in innovative high-growth sectors as set out in the UK’s Industrial Strategy. Rapidly expanding headcount allows scale-ups to absorb significant numbers of workers, creating high-skill, high-value employment.
